slides.title: Session assertion
slides.subtitle: A short-lived, audience-bound assertion for a pairwise user identity
slides.notes: To get a signed-out Session, a personal agent signs a Session assertion. This example shows what goes into one, and why each part is there.

slides.title: Why an assertion
slides.statement: The agent asks for a Session **as itself**, for a user, without impersonating the human.
slides.notes: The assertion identifies the agent, refers to the user only through an identifier made for this one company, names the exact authorization server it is meant for, and expires quickly.

slides.title: Who takes part

columns.heading: PAP host
columns.content: Builds the claims. The model only asks for a Session.

columns.heading: Pairwise ID store
columns.content: Keeps one stable, opaque subject per tenant, local user and company.

columns.heading: Reactor signer
columns.content: Signs the claims. The private key never leaves it.

slides.notes: The host builds the claims, a pairwise store gives it the user's subject for this company, and a Reactor signer turns the claims into a compact assertion. The company's authorization server then verifies it.

slides.title: How it flows

items.title: Resolve
items.detail: The pairwise subject for this company

slides.notes: The host resolves the subject, builds the claims and has them signed. The company checks the signature, that it is the audience, that the time window holds, and that it has never seen this jti. It answers with a signed-out Session Token.

slides.title: What each claim does

rows.label: sub
values: Two companies cannot correlate the user

rows.label: iat, exp
values: Bounds how long it is useful

slides.notes: Each claim limits the damage if an assertion escapes. The subject cannot be matched across companies, the audience pins it to one server, the lifetime is short, and the unique identifier lets the company refuse a second use.

slides.title: What the model sees

left.heading: Visible
items: Session ready, as an opaque reference

slides.notes: Signing goes through a Reactor capability, so private keys and compact assertions never become tool arguments or model output. The model learns the policy, not the values.

slides.title: Run it yourself
slides.cta: The Pydantic AI and Agent Runtimes examples build real Session claims and return only their policy
slides.notes: The small example stops at safe assertion policy: a Reactor plugin contributes a SQLite pairwise store, and the tool reports lifetime and bindings. The Session lifecycle example sends the assertion through a real token exchange.
